Learning Objectives
Outline surgical margins and determine appropriate goals for resection of soft-tissue sarcoma.
Assess physical examination findings and imaging studies to determine the appropriateness of
surgical resection of soft-tissue sarcoma.
Review extra-orthopaedic consultations and wound management strategies to optimize
outcomes of soft-tissue sarcoma resection.


Introduction
Soft-tissue sarcomas are a heterogenous group of mesoderm-derived cancers for which
nonsurgical management rarely is curative, thereby necessitating surgical excision as
part of definitive management. Because of their diverse histology, sizes, locations,
morphologies, preoperative therapies, and capacities for microscopic spread and
lymphatic involvement, academic and technical lessons to guide surgical management of
soft-tissue sarcomas cannot be distilled conveniently into easily digested morsels.
Instead, each tumor must be considered as a unique entity with regard to features
relevant to its excision that will maximize the oncologic and functional outcomes, which
often are antithetical.
This lesson is written from the standpoint of a surgeon planning surgical treatment for a
patient with a tumor already diagnosed, staged, and reviewed by a multidisciplinary
board and for whom appropriate neoadjuvant therapy has been provided.
Patient Communication and Navigation

Patient Communication and Navigation
Although often overlooked in surgeons’ desire to hone their technical skills,
communication with patients throughout the treatment process (and beyond) is
essential. Patients with any cancer diagnosis, particularly those with sarcoma, often are
directed through a battery of treatment options by multiple care teams. A high-value
role in this process is a centralized contact who can answer questions (or quickly obtain
answers from providers), shepherd patients through the process, and facilitate smooth
care transitions. This is particularly important in the preoperative period for patients
with sarcoma. Neoadjuvant care often is provided closer to home, and care team
awareness of a patient’s progress through treatment, the appropriate timing of
preoperative examination and restaging imaging, and the timing of surgical treatment
are critical. At many tertiary cancer centers, this role is facilitated by a nurse navigator.

Regardless of title or credentials, providing patients who have cancer with a reliable and
proactive contact should be considered part of the care process.
Preoperative Planning
Depending on a patient’s home address, the location of the surgical facility, and the assigned
neoadjuvant treatment regimen, a patient may return for surgical treatment weeks—even
months—after diagnosis. Therefore, an in-person visit with the patient before going to the
operating room is important.
Patients undergoing neoadjuvant therapy may experience weight changes, anorexia, cachexia,
and adverse skin changes, particularly associated with radiation therapy.
A patient with malnutrition or compromised skin is destined to have a suboptimal outcome;
therefore, global assessment of patients in this phase of care is critically important.
In general, this encounter may be best within the first week after completion of therapy.
Interval History and Physical Examination
Patients should be interviewed with respect to their habits and routines during neoadjuvant
treatment. Have they been eating well? Sleeping well? Adhering to their normal activity
routine? Any changes in bowel habits?
General appearance—Patients with weight loss or obvious cachexia should be further
interviewed about eating habits and undergo a consultation with a nutritionist preoperatively.
Skin—Patients, particularly those undergoing radiation therapy, must undergo a thorough
examination of the skin at and around the planned incision site. Skin sloughing or ulceration is
a contraindication to immediate surgical treatment and should elicit close follow-up to assess
for changes.
Neurovascular examination—A thorough examination for evidence of neurologic or vascular
compromise has critical importance to inform the surgeon of possible tumor growth and how
closely apposed essential nerves and vessels may be to the tumor. The neurovascular
examination also may have important medicolegal implications; therefore, documentation of
function before an intervention is in the best interests of all involved.
At the time of diagnosis, patients must be informed that any perception of neurologic or
vascular compromise should be reported immediately to the surgical team and prompt
immediate evaluation and, possibly, repeat imaging studies.

Imaging Studies
Imaging has advanced as much as any facet of medicine within the past 40 years and provides
a roadmap for surgical management. The advent and subsequent improvements of cross-
sectional imaging, particularly MRI, have revolutionized the ability to plan successful surgical
procedures and avoid or anticipate complications.
Plain radiographs may be the first imaging study available to orthopaedic oncologists.
Although rarely diagnostic, radiographs allow for evaluation of periosteal reaction or
remodeling that may occur because of local tumor progression.
In addition, lesions that occasionally feature mineralization, such as vascular tumors and
synovial sarcomas, may be visualized on radiographs, giving some indication of diagnosis.1,2
In general, radiographs have a minor role in surgical planning for soft-tissue sarcomas.
Ultrasonography may provide information about the size, depth, and consistency of soft-tissue
masses and may be used in the initial evaluation of a suspicious lesion.
Ultrasonography is particularly useful in distinguishing between cystic and solid components
of a mass and can be used to avoid necrotic or hemorrhagic regions during needle biopsy.
Malignant-appearing lesions are characterized by large size, irregular margins, tissue
heterogeneity, and propensity to invade through tissues, whereas benign lesions tend to be
smaller, superficially located, and homogeneous with well-defined margins.1
Similar to radiography, ultrasonography has a minor role in the surgical planning for soft-
tissue sarcomas.
CT provides the most detailed visualization of bony anatomy, osseous remodeling, periosteal
reactions, and areas of mineralization. Although inferior to MRI with regard to visualization of
soft-tissue anatomy, CT may be performed in patients in whom MRI is contraindicated.
CT also may be used to monitor for local recurrence and is comparable to MRI in the setting
of large recurrence. CT angiography with iodinated contrast agents can be performed to
evaluate lesion vascularity and vascular invasion.
CT also offers a very detailed view of the lungs and is commonly performed for surveillance
for distant metastases; however, the benefit of this enhanced resolution to patients has not
been documented definitively and currently is under prospective study.1,3
MRI is the highest value imaging modality for soft-tissue tumors for the purposes of
assembling a differential diagnosis and surgical planning.1 MRIs aid in tumor staging and
surgical planning via evaluation of tumor size, extension, assessment of neurovascular
involvement, and tumor necrosis.1,4

In general, soft-tissue masses are visible on MRI without the use of gadolinium-based
contrast agents; however, intravenous contrast administration allows for differentiation of
cystic structures from solid structures, visualization of vascular structures within a mass, and
identification of tumor necrosis.1,3
MRI also is the preferred imaging modality to monitor for local recurrence after resection.
The role of positron emission tomography (PET)—usually combined with CT (PET/CT)—is
evolving. PET does not have a defined role in the planning of definitive resections of soft-tissue
sarcoma; however, it is used at some institutions as a rule-out test for lymph node metastases
to determine if lymph node exploration is required as part of the definitive surgical
management.
PET also may be performed to assist with biopsy planning to determine areas of the tumor
that may yield viable, diagnostic tissue; however, MRI usually is sufficient for this purpose.
Preoperative Restaging
Staging studies guide medical and surgical treatment decisions and should be repeated if a
patient undergoes neoadjuvant treatment. A tumor that was previously deemed inoperable
based on its proximity to critical structures may have sufficiently decreased in size to allow for
successful wide local excision and reduced morbidity.
In the absence of neoadjuvant therapies, repeat staging studies may be helpful for surgical
planning if a lengthy workup period occurred preoperatively.
This determination may be best informed by tumor growth documented on physical
examination.
The authors of this lesson prefer not to surgically manage high-grade sarcoma in patients
with imaging studies performed more than 30 days preoperatively; patients who have low-
grade sarcoma without appreciable growth should undergo imaging studies within 3 months
preoperatively.
Preoperative Laboratory Studies
No specific laboratory studies are available to diagnose soft-tissue sarcoma; however, routine
hematologic, inflammatory, and nutritional tests are recommended as part of the initial
patient workup.
Several nonspecific changes in blood counts, including neutrophilia, leukocytosis, anemia,
monocytosis, and thrombocytosis, may occur in patients ultimately diagnosed with soft-tissue

sarcoma.
These findings occur in as many as 40% of patients and most frequently are noted in patients
with higher stage disease.5
Preoperative anemia (hemoglobin levels <13 g/dL in males and <12 g/dL in females) is a poor
prognostic indicator of disease-specific survival and overall survival in patients undergoing
surgical resection of soft-tissue sarcomas.6
Low absolute lymphocyte count (ALC; <1,000 cells/μL) confers a substantially lower 10-year
survival rate than normal ALC.
This trend worsens as ALC decreases further. Low ALC has been hypothesized to be
indicative of an immunologically suppressed state permissive to cancer growth.7
The neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio and platelet-lymphocyte ratio are two additional prognostic
indicators that may be analyzed preoperatively. Elevated pretreatment neutrophil-
lymphocyte ratio (≥2.5) and platelet-lymphocyte ratio (≥182) are independently associated
with decreased overall survival and disease-free survival.8,9
Pretreatment serum levels of various inflammatory markers also may be used to predict
outcomes. C-reactive protein is an acute phase reactant known to be elevated with multiple
cancer types.
Several studies demonstrate poorer local recurrence rates and poorer overall survival in
patients with high pretreatment serum C-reactive protein levels; however, no consensus
cutoff value exists in the literature, with reported threshold values ranging from 0.2 to 1
mg/dL.10,11
Similarly, elevated serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate are prognostic for poor overall
survival.12
Wound healing complications after resection of soft-tissue sarcomas are common and are
influenced by patient and treatment factors. Preoperative external beam radiation therapy is
associated with an increased risk of major postoperative wound complications, including those
necessitating a return to the operating room (débridement, surgical drainage, secondary
wound closure/grafting) and wound management without secondary surgery (seroma
aspiration, readmissions for intravenous antibiotic agents, persistent deep packing of the
wound).13-17
Poor preoperative nutritional status is a modifiable risk factor contributing to wound
complications in patients undergoing elective orthopaedic procedures. In addition,
pretreatment nutritional status is a known predictor of survival across many oncologic
subtypes.

Serum albumin level is a common proxy for nutritional status, and hypoalbuminemia (<3.5
mg/dL) is an independent risk factor for poor overall survival.18,19 The Onodera prognostic
nutritional index (OPNI) has been validated for use in predicting wound complications in
gastrointestinal cancers.
Recently, Kim et al20 demonstrated the utility of the Onodera prognostic nutritional index in
predicting wound complications after radiation therapy and surgical management of for soft-
tissue sarcomas in a small group of patients. The authors found that a score of less than45.4,
in which the Onodera prognostic nutritional index = (10 × albumin level [g/dL]) + (0.005 ×
total lymphocyte count), resulted in a 7.5 times higher risk of wound complication.
Other indices that combine inflammatory, coagulation, and nutrition laboratory values also
have demonstrated potential prognostic value.
According to Liang et al,21,22 the C-reactive protein level/albumin level ratio and the
fibrinogen level/albumin level ratio can be used to predict survival in patients with soft-tissue
sarcoma.
Patients with increased an C-reactive protein level/albumin level ratio (≥0.1035) or fibrinogen
level/albumin level ratio (≥0.0726) exhibit a shorter median survival time and a decreased 5-
year overall survival than those with low indices.
Preoperative Consultation
Working with colleagues is one of the joys of a career in academic medicine. Providers in other
specialties not only approach clinical challenges from different perspectives but also bring a
distinct skill set.
Plastic surgery
Plastic surgeons have great synergistic potential in the surgical management of soft-tissue
sarcomas.
Because of the frequent use of preoperative radiation therapy and occasional cytotoxic
chemotherapy, wound healing often is challenged after resection. Preemptive consultation
with a plastic surgeon may be helpful in avoiding wound healing problems and
downstream morbidity.
Little guidance exists with regard to appropriate indications for plastic surgery consultation;
therefore, the authors of this lesson generally advise “if you think about it, do it.”
Surgical oncology
Surgical oncologists receive training in two critical areas that most orthopaedic oncologists
lack: intra-abdominal and pelvic surgery and lymph node biopsy and dissection.

Appropriate indications for surgical oncology consultation usually can be explored during
multidisciplinary tumor board meetings but most often are indicated for tumors that
involve abdominopelvic regions and may require nodal exploration (eg, epithelioid
sarcoma).
Radiation oncology
Radiation oncologists should always be involved in the discussion of treatment for patients
with soft-tissue sarcoma; however, they rarely are in the operating room.
An exception to this occurs if brachytherapy is utilized. Indications for brachytherapy—
delivered via catheters placed intraoperatively—in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma are
evolving, based on the recommendations of the American Brachytherapy Society.
Brachytherapy for soft-tissue sarcomas should be considered in the following situations23:
Monotherapy for small tumors (<10 cm)
High-grade disease with substantial risk for local recurrence
Boost of radiation therapy after neoadjuvant treatment
Frail or elderly patients
Children (to limit dose and reduce risk of secondary malignancy)
Adjuvant Therapies and Treatment Timeline
Radiation therapy
Surgical resection is considered the only curative treatment option for soft-tissue sarcomas;
however, neoadjuvant and adjuvant radiation therapy routinely are used to improve surgical
margins and reduce the risk of tumor recurrence.
Preoperative and postoperative radiation therapy are associated with similar outcomes but
have different toxicity profiles. Preoperative radiation therapy is associated with a higher risk
of wound healing complications but requires lower doses (approximately 50 Gy) with fewer
long-term adverse effects.
Postoperative radiation therapy requires higher doses (approximately 66 Gy) and results in
fewer wound healing complications but poses a greater risk of tissue fibrosis and loss of
function.24,25
Postoperative radiation therapy and the administration of high-dose radiation therapy to the
bone have been identified as risk factors for pathologic fracture postoperatively.26-28
After preoperative radiation therapy, patients typically wait 3 to 6 weeks before undergoing
surgical treatment. Delayed resection allows time for a treatment response to occur and
normal tissues to heal; however, new evidence suggests that immediate resection after

completion of radiation therapy may reduce the risk of wound complications in addition to
substantially shortening the total duration of therapy. In a small retrospective analysis, Parsai
et al29 demonstrated favorable outcomes in patients who underwent a hypofractionated
radiation therapy regimen followed by surgical resection within 7 days. The observed rates of
wound healing complications were comparable to those of standard therapy at early follow-
up.
Chemotherapy
Systemic medical therapy generally is reserved for large and high-grade lesions; common
formulations include doxorubicin and ifosfamide.
The ideal neoadjuvant regimen will target micrometastases and reduce tumor burden such
that adequate surgical margins can be achieved.30
In addition, preoperative chemotherapy allows for identification of patients with chemo-
responsive tumors.
Individuals in whom metastatic disease develops while undergoing chemotherapy are
unlikely to benefit from a large resection and associated morbidity.
Surgical Strategy and Techniques
Surgical Margins
Nonsurgical therapies have limited curative effect; therefore, complete surgical resection is
considered a critical facet of soft-tissue sarcoma management. No objective consensus exists
with regard to the definition of a curative margin for soft-tissue sarcoma resection. The
medical literature indicates that the biologic behavior of various soft-tissue sarcomas is
heterogeneous and that although some subtypes rarely extend beyond their pseudocapsule,
others do so with abandon (eg, myxofibrosarcoma).
In 1980, Enneking et al31 proposed a classification system for surgical margins achieved during
resection of musculoskeletal sarcomas. Margins are classified based on proximity to the tumor
pseudocapsule, with the extent of the resection directly influencing the risk of local recurrence
(Figure 1). The four Enneking categories are as follows:
Intralesional—The surgical plane runs directly through the lesion, violating the tumor
pseudocapsule. This approach leaves microscopic, and in some instances, macroscopic,
tumor tissue at the margin. This approach is seldom indicated but may be used to debulk a
tumor that is otherwise not planned for complete resection.

Marginal—The surgical plane runs through the pseudocapsule, or reactive zone, surrounding
the tumor. Microscopic residual tumor tissue is assumed to be left behind within the
pseudocapsule. Marginal resections are associated with an elevated risk of local recurrence
(as high as 50%).32
Wide—The surgical plane runs through normal tissue surrounding the tumor, and the
dissection is maintained entirely within the involved compartment. The tumor and the
surrounding reactive zone are removed entirely. The risk of recurrence is low and is thought
to be related to skip lesions remaining in the compartment.
Radical—The resection removes the entire compartment (or compartments) affected by the
tumor.

resected or excised with these margins. (Reproduced from Mayerson JL, Scharschmidt TJ, Lewis
VO, Morris CD: Diagnosis and management of soft-tissue masses. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2014;22[11]:742-750.)

The Enneking classification system provides a conceptual framework for surgical planning but
lacks reproducibility, particularly as it relates to the assessment of margins achieved during
marginal and wide resections.33 Several new classification systems have since been
established that include microscopic assessment of surgical margins.
The R-classification system is based on macroscopic and microscopic evidence of malignancy
and stratifies resections into three categories.
R0: microscopically negative (no tumor cells found at the inked resection surface or intact
barrier)
R1: microscopically positive (microscopic contamination of the resection surface)
R2: grossly positive (macroscopic contamination, intralesional resection)
The Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) further adapted the R-classification system
to apply a 1-mm cutoff requirement for R0 resections. In this more stringent system, a rim of
normal tissue of 1 mm or more must be removed for the margin to be considered
negative.33 The UICC classification system is as follows:
R0: microscopically negative (resection margin ≥1 mm)
R1: microscopically positive (resection margin ≥1 mm)
R2: grossly positive
Margin status is an independent prognostic factor for local recurrence of soft-tissue sarcomas,
with more extensive resections correlating with a lower risk of tumor recurrence.
Although classification systems provide universal frameworks, substantial controversy exists
regarding adequate margin width, and differing study outcomes preclude formal
international consensus. Kainhofer et al34 demonstrated a decreased risk of local recurrence
after R0 resections based on the UICC classification system (1.3%) compared to the R-
classification system (2.1%).34
Conversely, Gundle et al35 showed no difference in R0 local recurrence (8%) between the two
classification systems. However, with the addition of the 1-mm margin requirement the
group reported a decrease in the local recurrence rate for R1 resections (12% versus 21%).
In addition, the increase in recurrence rate observed between R0 and R1 resections within
the UICC classification system was smaller than the increase observed in the R-classification
system, suggesting that the margin of less than 1 mm may be sufficient if combined with
adjunctive therapies. Similarly, Ahmad et al36 reported no difference in local recurrence or
overall survival for margin widths of 1 mm or less, 1 to 5 mm, and greater than 5 mm.
Certain histologic subtypes present additional challenges in determining adequate surgical
margins. For example, myxofibrosarcoma is an invasive soft-tissue sarcoma that demonstrates

an infiltrative growth pattern. The risk of local recurrence of myxofibrosarcoma has been
estimated to be as high as 30%, even in patients with negative margins.
A margin of 1 mm may be insufficient in patients with infiltrative lesions.33 Kikuta et al37
described a 28% rate of histologically positive margins despite a clear surgical plan for
resection with more than 3 cm margins. Local recurrence in this study was 21%.
In a study of patients with undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma and myxofibrosarcoma,
Iwata et al38 planned excisions with 2 to 3 cm margins as outlined by imaging studies.
Despite this, microscopically positive margins were noted in almost one-half of study
participants.
The extent of resection for sarcomas with infiltrative histology to achieve negative margins
has yet to be established, and intraoperative frozen sections may provide some clarity.
In some patients, a tumor may abut or encase important neurovascular or bony structures.
Resection of vascular structures may be warranted if bypass grafting can be achieved based on
consultation with a vascular surgeon (Video 1).
If the tumor violates the periosteum, periosteal stripping may be necessary to achieve the
desired margin.
If resection will require removal of more than 10 cm of periosteum, prophylactic
intramedullary fixation should be considered because of the increased risk of fracture.39
Even if sacrifice of surrounding structures is feasible, achieving completely negative surgical
margins is not always the goal of sarcoma resection.
Resection of critical structures should be completed only if the expected deficit associated
with removal results in a level of morbidity acceptable to the patient and the surgeon.
In a prospective study of patients who underwent excision of soft-tissue sarcomas, O’Donnell
et al40 found little evidence of adverse effects on the 5-year rate of local recurrence-free
survival in those with planned positive margins.
Obtaining negative margins (requiring resection of critical structures) only slightly improved
the 5-year rate of local recurrence-free survival.

Biopsy Tract Excision
Removal of the biopsy tract in continuity with the specimen is technically feasible in many
patients; however, the utility of this is a subject of debate.
Regardless of the selected biopsy technique, biopsy tracts that span a fascial layer provide
communication to the entire compartment, making tract excision likely ineffectual. In a
retrospective study, biopsy tract excision did not affect local recurrence41 (Video 2).

Extraneous Skin Excision
Soft-tissue sarcomas often serve as tissue expanders, possibly leaving redundant skin and
subcutaneous tissue after resection.
Leaving a fusiform skin and subcutaneous tissue paddle on the tumor may be beneficial in
several ways.
First, it creates an immediately identifiable orientation marking.
Second, if performed at the location at which the subcutaneous tissue is thinnest, it
reduces the likelihood of a positive margin.
Third, it reduces the need for thin subcutaneous flaps, thereby reducing the risk of wound
healing problems.
Fourth, it can provide cosmetic benefit by reducing redundant skin.
In excising skin with an extremity tumor, the authors of this lesson measure the circumference
of the surgical extremity at the apex of the tumor and the contralateral limb in the same
region. The difference between these measurements gives the surgeon an idea of the amount
of skin that may be excised without encountering wound tension problems, with the

understanding that the removal of some additional soft tissues as part of a wide excision likely
will enable additional skin to be removed without complications.
Instrument Selection
Although little or no data support instrumentation choices, certain instruments have proven
valuable.
Because of the nature of preoperative therapies to which many patients with soft-tissue
sarcoma are exposed, strict attention to techniques friendly to the skin and other tissues
should be used.
Examples include the use of a bipolar if in close proximity to high-value structures (nerves,
vessels, and the tumor itself),
Doppler to confirm vascular flow, and in the event of an emergency, easy access to vascular
instruments if performing surgery around major vessels
Intraoperative Frozen Section
Frozen section analysis of tissue samples may provide important intraoperative counsel to
surgeons if concern for the presence of tumor at the margins exists.
If appropriate sampling is performed, frozen section is associated with high sensitivity,
specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and accuracy in determining
the presence or absence of tumor.
The validity of frozen section is hindered by the sampling of tissue not amenable to frozen
section (fat, bone) and in the setting of extensive tumor necrosis.42-44
Wound Closure
Although the primary goal of surgical management of soft-tissue sarcoma is complete tumor
removal, surgeons must remain cognizant of the overall treatment goal: achieving maximal
oncologic control with the least functional impairment.45
Historically, many soft-tissue sarcomas were managed via amputation or radical resection.
Although these procedures were successful in providing local tumor control, they were
performed at the expense of residual limb function and failed to eliminate the risk of
metastatic disease in the future.45

Modern limb-salvage techniques achieve comparable oncologic control with superior
functional outcomes and highlight the importance of a multidisciplinary approach. If
possible, treatment should occur at specialized centers in coordination with a plastic surgeon
to optimize results.45-48
Wound closure should occur in layers if possible, ideally as a single-stage procedure
immediately after definitive tumor resection.
Drains and drain management
To further reduce the risk of postoperative wound complications and the potential for
hematoma and/or seroma formation, drains may be placed in the wound.
Placement of drains should be close to and, if possible, in-line with the incision to facilitate
excision of the tract in the event of tumor recurrence.39
Time to drain removal is patient specific but is influenced by several factors. In treatment
plans incorporating brachytherapy, removal of surgical drainage tubes should be deferred
until after the brachytherapy catheters are removed to minimize complications secondary
to catheter dislodgement.49 Otherwise, drains may be removed if output decreases
sufficiently.49,50
Wound Dressings
Temporary dressings for delayed reconstruction
Although primary wound closure is preferred, this is not always possible because of the
volume of tissue removed or poor confidence in negative margins after excision.
Intraoperative frozen sections of tissue are poor predictors of final negative margins,
necessitating staged closure after final histologic evaluation of margins.51
Two common methods of wound coverage between staged procedures include meshed skin
allograft with petroleum impregnated gauze overlaying the graft, bolstered by a dense foam
stapled or sutured into place to reduce shear stress or a vacuum-assisted closure device.52
Incisional vacuum dressings
Incisional vacuum dressings (placement of the vacuum sponge over the closed surgical
incision) decrease postoperative deep infections, wound dehiscence, and other wound
complications, particularly in patients with lower extremity soft-tissue sarcoma.14,53-59
Use of this technique affects wound healing via indirect and direct methods.59-65
Although sub-atmospheric pressure promotes malignant tissue growth,66 no evidence
supports concerns that this therapy increases the risk of tumor recurrence.53,58,59,67

Postoperative Management
Wound Care
Wound management considerations and follow-up
No consensus exists with regard to the timing of follow-up visits beyond the immediate
postoperative period dedicated to close monitoring of wound healing and the management
of rehabilitation.
Follow-up visits should be scheduled using a stepwise, progressively increasing time interval.
In general, sutures/staples should be removed 7 to 10 days postoperatively for the chest,
fingers, hand, and lower extremities; sutures/staples should be removed 10 to 14 days
postoperatively for the back, forearm, and foot.68,69
Prolonged suture retention may lead to suture marks, local tissue reaction, and scarring,
whereas premature suture removal increases the risk of reopening of the incision.68,69
The authors of this lesson see patients for follow-up approximately 10 to 14 days
postoperatively for wound evaluation.
Functional Limitations
Soft-tissue reconstruction requirements
If split-thickness skin grafts are used for wound closure in areas subject to shear (axilla,
antecubital fossa, or popliteal fossa), a splint should be placed before exiting the operating
room.
Splinting aids in preserving limb function and helps prevent hemorrhage, hematoma
formation, wound dehiscence, and abnormal scar formation.70,71
In addition, the surgical extremity should be elevated for 4 to 5 days postoperatively to
reduce edema.
Early mobilization is necessary to preserve function; however, great care must be taken to
prevent excessive motion that jeopardizes graft success and/or adequate wound healing.
Activity precautions should remain in place for approximately 1 month postoperatively to
optimize graft success.
Ingrowth-requiring reconstruction
Occasionally, a soft-tissue sarcoma may abut long bones, and stripping of the periosteum
may be performed to attain adequate margins.

Risk factors for postoperative pathologic femur fracture include periosteum stripping of
more than 10 cm, patient age, female sex, tumor size, tumor location, postoperative
radiation, and administration of high-dose radiation therapy to the bone.26-28
Prophylactic internal fixation may be indicated in certain scenarios, and activity restrictions
may be appropriate for extended periods because of poorer bone healing and greater risk of
nonunion after radiation therapy.
Non–ingrowth-requiring reconstruction
Patients who undergo reconstruction that can be closed primarily and do not warrant
prophylactic internal fixation generally may return to activity as tolerated.
Summary
Soft-tissue sarcomas are a heterogeneous group of rare tumors for which curative
management generally requires complete surgical excision. Management of these tumors is
best performed at a tertiary cancer center with an experienced and multidisciplinary team.
Surgical strategies must be patient- and tumor-specific; therefore, each patient must be
considered individually. Thorough preoperative planning with appropriate and recent imaging
studies, extra-orthopaedic consultations, and tissue-friendly techniques will optimize the
likelihood of success.
